title: the DSG underground geography and theories

banner.title: THE DSG UNDERGROUND GEOGRAPHY AND THEORIES, R531: printed pp. 69-71 (pdf 70-72) - the second DM-section round, two children: the underground geography - domains in three dimensions (the total accessible area equaling the ground area of a large nation, the campaign-by-campaign world building, the 1,000-mile sample region; the surface terrain - the water-filled sea tunnels with their permanent-magic rationale, the stale dead-end air pockets, the water table, the higher-altitude mountain domains with explorers resurfacing at the mountain base, and the granite-versus-limestone seabeds; the temperature - the geothermal plant growth, the drow and duergar warm lairs making intelligent encounters likelier near heat, and the slow convection exploited by ventilation tunnels; the humidity - the brittle dried formations, the steamy scavenger-prized slippery rock, the dusty low-humidity areas, and the ever-changing erosion with its cave-ins and rock slides; the size - the creature-size limits of the three-foot halfling tunnels, the avoided unsupported caverns stretching a mile wide, the drow-duergar-derro support columns and permanenced spells, and the jermalaine-pech small-tunnel defense; the origin - the irregular natural caverns, the duergar-svirfneblin domed cities with their straight miles-long tunnels and ornate stonework, the drow-kuo-toa preference for conquering duergar lairs, and the mind flayer-myconid natural caverns; and the access and egress - the fresh air near surface connections, the no-access air shafts of the arctic example, and the easy-access raiders orcs, goblins and kobolds versus the deep cultures shunning the outside world), and the theories on the nature of the underground (the DM-decides frame and the sage-knowledge role playing; the hollow earth theory with its variants - the inner world of flyers and levitators cloaked in darkness with volcanic light, the lava-rain fire world, the far-fetched inner shell, and the Plane of Air connection; the Swiss cheese theory with the goblin-hobgoblin-orc ubiquity argument, the failed expeditions, and the unexploited connections; the isolated pockets theory with its forced-migration goblin-slave explanation; and the partial connection theory with its fire and water blocks and the later-sealed traversable pasts)
banner.provenance: the DSG scan (archive.org item advanced-dungeons-dragons-1st-edition), pdf = printed + 1; the text read from the IA djvu OCR (djvu.txt lines ~8902-9268) with the pdf Acrobat-Capture layer as the second read (idx 163-168 = the printed pp. 69-71 windows; the odd image-heavy interleaves hold no text in Capture); the compiled-tables appendix has no reprint of this prose. A CLEAN-READ ROUND: both machine reads agree on every load-bearing number - the 1,000-mile diameter, the three-foot tunnels, the hundreds-of-feet ceilings, and the mile-side-to-side caverns; the only garbles are the standing glyph classes (the Cyrillic-lead djvu noise in the page headers). SEAMS: the R530 underground environment (the oxygen circulation the air-shaft geography elaborates), the R521-R524 mining rounds (the duergar and svirfneblin excavators), the Monster Manual cultures, the DMG inner planes (the Plane of Air connection), and the R503 re-grain. Nothing auto-credits.
banner.sentinel: A prose round: no tables pin. The numbers pin as consts per the R508 convention: the 1,000-mile sample-region diameter, the 3-foot halfling tunnels, and the 1-mile-wide largest caverns. The rest pins as prose bools: the geography factors (the frame, the surface terrain, the temperature, the humidity, the size, the origin, the access and egress) and the four theories with the DM-decides frame. The R530/R521-R524/MM/DMG/R503 seams are noted; nothing auto-credits.

consts.name: dngrRegionDiaMiles
consts.comment: the typical underground geography area detailed for the DM is about 1,000 miles in diameter and several dozen miles in depth, adaptable to his campaign.

consts.name: dngrHalflingTunnelFt
consts.comment: a group of halfling explorers does not worry about encountering ogres in a network of three-foot-wide tunnels - the expanse of an area limits the sizes of creatures encountered there.

consts.name: dngrBigCavernMileWide
consts.comment: some of the largest underground caverns have ceilings soaring hundreds of feet and stretch as much as a mile from side to side.

bools.name: dngrLargeNationArea
bools.comment: the total area of all the caverns, dungeons and tunnels equals the ground area of a large nation - this accessible total is the underground world that awaits the players, its layout to be well conceived and thoroughly understood by the DM.

bools.name: dngrCampaignByCampaign
bools.comment: habitable underground terrain extends beneath much of the campaign world, but mapping an entire world of caverns is impractical - the DM handles the creation on a campaign-by-campaign basis, the sample-area patterns adapted to his needs.

bools.name: dngrSeaWaterFilled
bools.comment: a network of tunnels or caverns beneath a body of water is nearly always water-filled; air requires a rationale - permanent magic holding the water at bay.

bools.name: dngrTrappedAirStale
bools.comment: air pockets trapped in dead-end corridors cannot circulate, and hence are stale and of limited use for air-breathing creatures.

bools.name: dngrWaterTable
bools.comment: even areas below dry land may be water-filled: all areas contain a water table, a level below which all openings are filled with water, and without steady drainage it can make entire stretches of caverns uninhabitable.

bools.name: dngrMountainDomainsHigher
bools.comment: a domain beneath mountains may hold dungeons or caverns actually higher in altitude than many surrounding lands - explorers move deeper and deeper and abruptly return to the surface at the base of the mountain range.

bools.name: dngrGraniteLimestone
bools.comment: mountains and other solid-granite areas are much less likely to be penetrated by caves than the vast limestone bedrock expanses beneath the plains and forests - former seabeds, the most susceptible to natural cave formation - though excavated areas can be discovered anywhere.

bools.name: dngrGeothermalPlants
bools.comment: when geothermal energy is present, caverns tend to be more crowded with subterranean plants than cooler regions are.

bools.name: dngrWarmLairHeatRaces
bools.comment: intelligent races, particularly the drow and the duergar, seek out the warmer caverns for their lairs and cities - so the chance of encountering intelligent denizens is significantly higher around sources of underground heat.

bools.name: dngrConvectionVentilation
bools.comment: warm temperatures circulate air, heated air rising and cool fresh air drawn in; the natural convection is slow and inefficient, so intelligent races often excavate ventilation tunnels to exploit it, giving modified areas a good supply of fresh air.

bools.name: dngrDryCaveBrittle
bools.comment: if a cave dries up, its stalactites, stalagmites and all exposed surfaces grow extremely brittle and eventually turn to dust.

bools.name: dngrSteamyScavengerRock
bools.comment: high humidity with warm temperatures creates a steamy environment highly prized by certain scavengers - the rock very slippery, often coated with lichen, mold or other slimy matter.

bools.name: dngrLowHumidityDusty
bools.comment: underground areas of extremely low humidity, regardless of temperature, tend to be very dusty.

bools.name: dngrErosionHazards
bools.comment: water flowing through an area constantly erodes its bed so the area itself is always changing - often leading to cave-ins and rock slides, hazards not common in drier regions.

bools.name: dngrSizeLimitsCreatures
bools.comment: the expanse of an area determines a great many characteristics, most obviously the physical limitations on the sizes of creatures encountered there.

bools.name: dngrHugeCavernsAvoided
bools.comment: unless a huge cavern is magically or physically supported, intelligent creatures avoid it when seeking living quarters - even a minor earthquake, tremor or landslide could cave in a section of the ceiling catastrophically.

bools.name: dngrSupportColumnsSpells
bools.comment: the drow, duergar and derro do prefer large underground areas for their communities, but are careful to prevent disasters - support columns the most common precaution, with permanenced magical spells also serving against cave-ins.

bools.name: dngrSmallTunnelDefense
bools.comment: creatures such as the jermalaine and pech choose small, constricted tunnel networks as living quarters - their small size is their greatest defense in such locations; other underground creatures adapt to both small and large lairs.

bools.name: dngrNaturalIrregular
bools.comment: naturally eroded or developed places - caverns, lava caves - vary widely in size and shape, earmarked by irregular walls, ceilings and floors, sometimes so rough, steep or constricted that travel on foot is virtually impossible.

bools.name: dngrDuergarSmoothCities
bools.comment: the lairs of the duergar and svirfneblin are the most smoothly carved regions of the underworld - often a large central cavern developed into a virtual domed city with individual residences excavated into the cavern walls.

bools.name: dngrStraightMileTunnels
bools.comment: the skilled miners are capable of digging a perfectly straight tunnel many miles long, or of creating ornate stonework decorations.

bools.name: dngrDrowConquerLairs
bools.comment: races such as the drow and kuo-toa have limited excavation ability and much prefer to discover a fine duergar lair, overcome the gray dwarves defenses and claim it for their own; the mind flayers and myconids show no interest or ability in excavation, living in natural caverns or abandoned dungeons.

bools.name: dngrAirShaftsNoAccess
bools.comment: fresh air is much more plentiful in areas with some direct connection to the surface - though air can flow through shafts and tunnels that do not allow creatures easy access, the miles-deep arctic ventilation shafts a good example.

bools.name: dngrEasyAccessRaiders
bools.comment: areas allowing easy access to the surface are populated by creatures that occasionally leave to raid or trade - orcs, goblins and kobolds the good examples - while most Underdark cultures dwell so deep they need not worry about the outside world, shunning the surface and its intrusion alike.

bools.name: dngrDmDecidesTheory
bools.comment: each theory was proposed by adventurers or sages and has its own merits - which if any are correct is the DMs decision, consistent with his overall campaign plans.

bools.name: dngrSageKnowledge
bools.comment: the theories are not common knowledge but are regarded much as an advanced scientific hypothesis is today - not secret to the sages, but not of broad popular interest; player characters must seek out knowledgeable NPCs and role play for the information.

bools.name: dngrHollowEarthTheory
bools.comment: the hollow earth theory holds that the surface is a mere crust over a vast open space where life forms exist almost completely isolated from the surface - no adventurer is known to have visited the inner earth, all reports originating from the deepest cultures.

bools.name: dngrHollowInnerWorld
bools.comment: some stories maintain a vast atmosphere beneath the crust with a small version of our own world at its middle - only creatures that can fly or levitate for long periods could travel between the worlds, and the inner earth is presumably cloaked in utter darkness though savage volcanic bouts light up great tracts of it.

bools.name: dngrHollowLavaRain
bools.comment: other versions hold that columns of fiery lava fall from the outer earth as a rain of fire onto the inner earths surface - the temperature very high, hosting only creatures with a considerable liking for or resistance to fire.

bools.name: dngrHollowShellVariant
bools.comment: another theory holds the entire center hollow with the outer earth a thin shell - creatures living on the inside looking up to the center - considered one of the more far-fetched explanations.

bools.name: dngrHollowAirCenter
bools.comment: a variation keeps the air-filled center but denies creatures walking upside down on the inner shell: the center is home only to flying and levitating creatures, and is in fact a prime point of connection between the Plane of Air and our plane.

bools.name: dngrSwissCheeseTheory
bools.comment: the Swiss cheese theory holds the world fundamentally solid with no massive hollow core, but with enough caves, caverns and artificial passageways for an individual to travel anywhere under the world.

bools.name: dngrGoblinUbiquity
bools.comment: the supporting argument is the widespread occurrence of goblins, hobgoblins and orcs - none liking to travel overland, so their wanderings must have occurred through a vast tunnel network; the mirrored characteristics of distant goblins prove nothing, since they might have migrated overland or received common traits from the same source - an evil deity, for example.

bools.name: dngrFailedExpeditions
bools.comment: many adventurers have embarked to prove the theory - most failed to return, and the survivors report only failure: routes that dead-ended, circled back upon themselves, or led to the surface near the starting point.

bools.name: dngrUnexploitedConnections
bools.comment: if connections between most Underdark realms exist, the fact is unexploited by its denizens - perhaps the passages are too small for great numbers, the habitable regions too far apart, or strife has prevented large-scale movements.

bools.name: dngrIsolatedPocketsTheory
bools.comment: the isolated pockets theory is the least imaginative but fits most closely with present observations: each discovered underground region is an area unto itself, with no subterranean connections to any other.

bools.name: dngrForcedMigration
bools.comment: the contrary evidence - cultural similarities between widely separated populations - is explained as migration over the surface or the influence of a deity unbounded by geography; sunlight-hating creatures could have been forced to migrate overland, as goblins enslaved by humans who escaped into the dungeons, keeping their ancestors traditions.

bools.name: dngrPartialConnectionTheory
bools.comment: the partial connection theory, common among the most knowledgeable students, maintains connections between all or most underground regions but stops short of easy accessibility: the routes are treacherous and often impassable.

bools.name: dngrFireWaterBlocks
bools.comment: fire - volcanic activity, lava, steam - is commonly suggested as a block to these passages, traversable only by creatures with powerful fire resistance; water is the other common obstacle, regions beneath the deepest seas unlikely to hold breathable air - a region traversable in the distant past could later have been filled with water or split by volcanic fire.
